headline: High-risk pair: shared MCP/browser/network surfaces create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can ingest and act on external content via browsers, MCP, and tool outputs. LightAgent exposes MCP over stdio/SSE and runtime hooks; oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and team messaging. That creates a plausible default path for attacker-controlled content to cross from one agent into the other and be parsed as instructions.
conditions: IF either agent forwards raw web or tool output into the other's prompt without provenance filtering, injection is possible.
IF a shared MCP server or message channel is enabled between them, attacker-controlled content can bridge the pair.
mitigations: Disable shared MCP/message channels between the agents.
Add provenance tags and strip instruction-like text before forwarding outputs.
Route inter-agent content through a fixed schema, not free text.
Review browser-sourced content before it reaches the other agent.
requires-engineering: add content provenance enforcement at the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent touches user conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and secrets; oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data. Both have broad network egress and browser access, so if they share a workspace or prompt chain, sensitive material can be exfiltrated to third parties by default.
conditions: IF the two agents share a workspace or clipboard, sensitive data can move from one agent to the other.
IF either agent sends its context or file contents to external APIs, leakage can extend beyond the local environment.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials per agent.
Disable automatic file-content upload where possible.
Keep secrets out of shared prompts and logs.
Rotate any exposed provider auth data immediately.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support subprocesses, browsers, and broad network egress, and both can run multiple instances. LightAgent also uses MCP and oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks, so overlapping writes or concurrent tool actions can conflict if they target the same files, sessions, or external resources.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable directory or repo, write conflicts can occur.
IF both agents modify shared MCP or browser state concurrently, one can overwrite the other's changes.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize writes to shared resources.
Disable concurrent edits to the same repo or config files.
Use per-agent browser profiles.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent can emit tool results, workflow state, and provenance metadata, while oh-my-openagent exposes team_send_message and task creation APIs. If oh-my-openagent treats LightAgent output as authoritative, errors can cascade into messages or tasks without verification, turning a bad intermediate result into downstream action.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent consumes LightAgent output without a verification step, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF team_send_message or task creation is wired to LightAgent outputs, the cascade can trigger external actions.
mitigations: Require human review before sending messages or creating tasks.
Add a verification step for all LightAgent-derived facts.
Limit LightAgent outputs to structured fields with confidence markers.
Log source provenance alongside every downstream action.
requires-engineering: implement policy gates for action-taking APIs.

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent explicitly handles user conversations, long-term memory, and secrets, while oh-my-openagent handles project code, session history, and provider auth data. The profiles do not document residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if regulated data is routed through the pair; uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated personal data or secrets are routed through both agents, residency or retention obligations may diverge.
IF one agent logs or retains data longer than the other, deletion/export obligations can fail.
mitigations: Avoid routing regulated data through both agents.
Review retention and logging settings for each agent.
Keep secrets in a dedicated vault, not prompts.
Document data residency for each deployment.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows across both systems.
